record.title: Independent note estimates extreme practical thresholds for OpenAI’s claimed ETH algorithm
record.summary: A version 1 arXiv note dated Oct 31 explains OpenAI’s claimed subexponential exact-counting result and reports that constants extracted by the authors from the Oct 25 tensor-contraction proof leave its certified running time above brute force until input sizes far beyond anything representable. The note explicitly preserves the asymptotic claim and says its separate structural limits cover the clause-product interpolation route, not the sharper parity and tensor-contraction routes. These are author-reported calculations, not independently verified results or a refutation of the headline theorem.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Dias and Lima posted version 1 of their note on arXiv on 2026-10-31, analyzing the constants and scope of OpenAI’s claimed ETH-refuting exact-counting algorithm.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their extraction from the Oct 25 tensor-contraction proof leaves the certified running time above 2^n for bounded-density inputs unless log2(n+m) exceeds about 1.03×10^9, and for random 3-CNF at the satisfiability threshold unless log2 n exceeds about 5.3×10^11.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors say their structural limits apply to the clause-product interpolation route under their stated cost model; they explicitly say that the parity form and tensor-contraction proof escape those limits.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: This review did not independently reproduce the authors’ constants or proof analysis. The note itself preserves the asymptotic subexponential claim and does not establish that OpenAI’s theorem is false.

evidence_gaps.description: The note’s constant extraction from the Oct 25 tensor-contraction proof has not been independently reproduced.
The note explicitly leaves the sharper parity and tensor-contraction routes outside its structural lower bounds.

brief.importance_rationale: If the constant extraction holds, it changes how researchers interpret the practical significance of an asymptotic ETH result at representable input sizes, while leaving the asymptotic theorem intact.
limitations: The constants are the authors’ extraction from a proof whose theorem remains asymptotic; the note says it certifies no feasible bounded-density speedup under the analyzed bound, not that no faster algorithm exists.
The clause-product structural limits apply under the paper’s specified cost model and do not cover the preprint’s parity or tensor-contraction routes.

The authors report using Claude Opus 5.5 for reading, derivation, code, verification and drafting, and a separate instance for draft review; their code and proof were not independently audited in this review.
No independent mathematical reproduction or review was obtained in this activation.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that the tensor-contraction proof certifies no bounded-density speedup over 2^n until log2(n+m) exceeds about 1.03×10^9, and that their clause-product scheme limits follow under the stated cost model.
technical.demonstrated_result: The Oct 31 arXiv v1 note is publicly available and explicitly distinguishes its finite-size constant analysis from the asymptotic claim; it also states that its clause-product limits do not cover the parity and tensor-contraction routes. The mathematical conclusions were not independently validated in this review.
technical.mechanism: The authors extract explicit constants from OpenAI’s recursive Boolean tensor-network contraction proof and analyze a distinct clause-product interpolation scheme under an evaluation cost model that charges its enumerated groups, measurement tuples and restricted sums.
technical.regime: Author analysis of a versioned OpenAI Oct 25 manuscript; bounded-density formulas and a random 3-CNF threshold case; a specified cost model for the separate clause-product interpolation scheme.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction of the constants was performed. The paper reports small code-backed experiments and AI-assisted derivation, and explicitly states that its limits do not cover the sharper parity/tensor-contraction routes.
technical.strongest_baseline: The note compares its extracted bounds with brute-force 2^n counting and analyzes the Oct 25 OpenAI preprint’s stated theorem and proof routes.

brief.title: Independent note estimates extreme practical thresholds for OpenAI’s claimed ETH algorithm
brief.why_it_matters: If the authors’ extraction is sound, it qualifies the practical interpretation of a major asymptotic complexity result: the claimed subexponential rate may have no certified advantage at feasible input sizes. The note does not refute the asymptotic claim, and its narrower structural results do not cover the sharper proof routes.

other.title: OpenAI releases a claimed AI-generated refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis with Lean formalization
other.summary: OpenAI reports that an internal model produced a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), then released a natural-language manuscript and Lean formalization. The linked Lean scope describes a subexponential exact-counting bound for fixed-k canonical k-CNF formulas, a formalized statement that would contradict ETH if its definitions and scope match the standard conjecture. OpenAI says an external group led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams will examine the result; the group’s participation is not certification. Independent mathematical review, a reproduced build and practical algorithmic consequences remain unestablished.
